items.q: A spider has 8 legs. How many legs do 7 spiders have?
items.hint: 7 spiders is 7 groups of 8 legs. You can count in 8s seven times, or work out 8 × 7.
steps: Each spider has 8 legs, and there are 7 spiders, so it is 7 groups of 8.

slips.say: 15 is 8 + 7. That adds the two numbers. Here every spider has its own 8 legs, so we need 7 groups of 8.
48 is 6 spiders. Count one more group of 8.
64 is 8 × 8, which is 8 spiders. Take away one group of 8.

tpl.q: A spider has 8 legs. How many legs do {n} spiders have?
tpl.hint: {n} spiders is {n} groups of 8 legs. Count in 8s {n} times.
steps: Each spider has 8 legs, and there are {n} spiders, so it is {n} groups of 8.

items.q: You know 5 × 9 = 45. Use it to find 6 × 9.
items.hint: 6 groups of 9 is just one more group of 9 than 5 groups of 9.

slips.say: 45 is 5 × 9, the fact we started with. Now add one more group of 9.
Add the whole 9, not just 5.
63 is 7 × 9, one group too many.

tpl.q: You know 5 × {k} = {f}. Use it to find 6 × {k}.
tpl.hint: 6 groups of {k} is one more group of {k} than 5 groups.

items.q: 63 apples are packed into boxes of 7 apples, with none left over. Count in 7s (7, 14, 21, …) to find how many boxes there are.
items.hint: Count in 7s until you reach 63 and keep track of how many 7s you said.
steps: That is 9 numbers, so there are 9 boxes.

slips.say: 56 is 7 × 8, one box short of 63 apples. Keep counting to 63.
7 is the number of apples in one box. We need how many boxes.
8 boxes hold 56 apples. We need 63, so one more box.

tpl.q: {t} apples are packed into boxes of 7 apples, with none left over. Count in 7s to find how many boxes there are.
tpl.hint: Count in 7s until you reach {t}, and keep track of how many 7s you said.
steps: You say {m} numbers, so there are {m} boxes.

items.q: Find 9 × 7 by working out 10 × 7 and taking away one 7.
items.hint: 10 × 7 is easy. 9 groups is one group fewer than 10 groups.
steps: 9 × 7 is one group of 7 fewer than 10 × 7.

slips.say: 77 is 11 × 7. We need to take a 7 away from 70, not add one.
70 is 10 × 7. Now take away one 7.

tpl.q: Find 9 × {k} by working out 10 × {k} and taking away one {k}.
tpl.hint: 10 × {k} = {t}. 9 groups is one group of {k} fewer.

items.q: Draw 6 rows of 8 dots. How many dots are there? (Turn your page sideways: it shows 8 rows of 6 dots. Do you get the same number?)
items.hint: Count the dots row by row, or count in 8s six times.
steps: 6 rows of 8 dots is 6 groups of 8.
Turning the page gives 8 rows of 6 dots. It is 48 again, so 6 × 8 and 8 × 6 give the same answer.

slips.say: 14 is 6 + 8. Each of the 6 rows has 8 dots, so we need 6 groups of 8.
42 is 6 × 7. Each row has 8 dots, not 7.
56 is 7 × 8: one row too many.

tpl.q: Draw {r} rows of {c} dots. How many dots are there?
tpl.hint: Count the dots row by row, or count in {c}s {r} times.
steps: {r} rows of {c} dots is {r} groups of {c}.
Turning the page gives {c} rows of {r}, with the same {ans} dots.

items.q: Count in 6s from 6 up to 60: 6, 12, 18, 24, … Look only at the LAST digit of each number. Which last digits do you see?
items.hint: Write the numbers out (6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60) and underline each last digit.
steps: Only 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 appear, and they repeat in the same order every 5 numbers.

items.q: The digits of every answer in the 9 times table add up to 9 (18: 1 + 8 = 9). Which of these numbers are in the 9 times table?
items.hint: Add the digits of each number. Does it make 9?
steps: So 54 and 72 are in the 9 times table. (54 = 9 × 6 and 72 = 9 × 8.)

items.q: What is the last digit of 8 × 8 × 8? Use last digits only.
items.hint: 8 × 8 = 64. Keep only the last digit (4), then multiply by 8 again.
steps: So the last digit of 8 × 8 × 8 is 2. (Check: 8 × 8 × 8 = 512.)

slips.say: 4 is the last digit of 8 × 8. There is one more 8 to multiply by.
8 is just the starting number. Multiply the last digit of 8 × 8 by 8 once more.

tpl.q: What is the last digit of {a} × {a} × {a}? Use last digits only.
tpl.hint: {a} × {a} ends in {p}. Keep only that last digit, then multiply by {a} again.

items.q: Ravi says: "Every answer in the 6 times table is even." Is he right?
items.hint: Look at 6, 12, 18, 24 … Then think: can 6 groups always be shared into pairs?
steps: Looking at a few examples does not prove it. Here is why it is always true: 6 groups can always be made into 3 pairs of groups, so nothing is left over.
For example 6 × 7 = 3 × 14 = 42. So Ravi is right.

slips.say: Try the 6 times table: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 … Can you find an odd one? Think about why 6 groups can always be paired.

items.q: Find ALL the 2-digit numbers that can be divided exactly by 7 and whose digits add up to 10. Type them with a comma between, like 12, 34.
items.hint: List the 2-digit numbers in the 7 times table (14, 21, 28 …) and add the digits of each one.
steps: The 2-digit numbers in the 7 times table: 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49, 56, 63, 70, 77, 84, 91, 98.

slips.say: 28 works. Is there another one? Keep listing the 7 times table up to 98.
91 works. Is there another one? Check the smaller numbers in the table too.

items.q: Ben multiplies a number by 6. His answer ends in 4. What could the last digit of his number be? Find all the possible digits.
items.hint: Try each last digit 0 to 9 times 6, and see which answers end in 4.
steps: So the last digit could be 4 or 9.

slips.say: 4 works (6 × 4 = 24). Is there another digit? Try all the digits up to 9.
9 works (6 × 9 = 54). Is there another digit?

items.q: How many numbers from 1 to 200 can be divided exactly by both 6 and 9?
items.hint: A number that works for both is in the 6 times table AND the 9 times table. Find the smallest one, then keep adding it.
steps: The 6 times table: 6, 12, 18 …   The 9 times table: 9, 18, 27 … The first number in both is 18.
So the numbers are in the 18 times table: 18, 36, 54, 72, 90, 108, 126, 144, 162, 180, 198.
Count them: 11 numbers (and 18 × 12 = 216 is more than 200).

slips.say: 33 is how many numbers up to 200 are in the 6 times table. The number must be in the 9 times table too.
22 is how many are in the 9 times table. The number must be in the 6 times table too.
Check 198: it is 18 × 11, and it is less than 200, so it counts.

tpl.q: How many numbers from 1 to {N} can be divided exactly by both 6 and 9?
tpl.hint: The numbers in both tables are the 18 times table. How many 18s fit in {N}?
steps: The first number in both tables is 18, so they are the 18 times table.
We need how many 18s fit in {N}.

items.q: Siti says the answer to 6 × 7 × 8 × 9 ends in 4. Is she right? Use last digits only.
items.hint: Multiply two at a time and keep only the last digit each time.
steps: 6 × 9 = 54, which ends in 4. So Siti is right. (6 × 7 × 8 × 9 = 3024.)

slips.say: Check step by step: 6 × 7 = 42 (ends 2), 2 × 8 = 16 (ends 6), 6 × 9 = 54 (ends 4).

items.q: Mei has fewer than 100 sweets. She can share them equally among 6 friends, among 9 friends and among 4 friends, with none left over each time. Find ALL the numbers of sweets she could have.
items.hint: The number must be in the 6, the 9 and the 4 times tables. Find the smallest, then see how the others follow.
steps: Which of these are also in the 4 times table? 36 (4 × 9) and 72 (4 × 18).
So Mei has 36 or 72 sweets. They are 36 apart: after the first, the pattern repeats every 36.

slips.say: 36 works. Is there another one under 100?
72 works. Is there a smaller one?
18 is in the 6 and 9 tables, but 4 does not divide 18 exactly. Check with 4.

items.q: I am a 3-digit number less than 200. I can be divided exactly by 7 and by 9. My digits add up to 9. What number am I?
items.hint: A number in both the 7 and 9 tables is in the 63 times table. List those below 200.

slips.say: 189 is in both tables, but its digits add up to 18. Check the digits of the other one.
63 is only a 2-digit number. We need 3 digits.

items.q: Make up your own riddle: "I am a 2-digit number in the ___ times table …" Write 2 or 3 clues (odd or even, the digits, between two numbers). List the table to check that only ONE number fits.
items.hint: Pick a secret number first, then write clues that are true for it. Then list the table and cross out numbers that break a clue.
steps: Check: your secret number is in the table and every clue is true for it.
List the table. Cross out every number that breaks a clue. Exactly one number should be left.
Example: "I am a 2-digit number in the 7 times table. I am odd. My digits add up to 10." The odd 2-digit numbers in the 7 table are 21, 35, 49, 63, 77, 91, and only 91 has digits adding to 10.
